opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most foreseeable pathway to really rapid progress within a year is AI systems automating a large fraction of AI research and engineering itself.

Right now, a huge share of what frontier labs do is fairly concrete software and research engineering: writing training infrastructure, running experiments, debugging, tuning hyperparameters, analyzing results, trying small algorithmic tweaks. These are the tasks where current models are improving fastest, partly because they're verifiable. You can check whether the code runs, whether the loss went down, whether the benchmark improved. So it's quite plausible that within a year or so, models go from being a useful assistant to doing a meaningful chunk of that work fairly autonomously.

Once that happens, you get a feedback loop. Labs have enormous compute for running these agents, and you can run many copies in parallel, faster than humans, around the clock. Even if each copy is somewhat worse than a top researcher, the sheer quantity of labor could substantially speed up algorithmic progress. Better algorithms then make the next generation of AI researchers more capable, and so on.

Compute is a real constraint, since you still need to run experiments and you can't scale hardware overnight. But historically a lot of progress has come from algorithmic and efficiency improvements, and those are exactly what automated research labor would target. So I'd say: watch how well AI systems do on long-horizon, agentic software and ML engineering tasks. If that keeps improving at the rate we've seen, the step from "helpful coding tool" to "substantially accelerating AI R&D" could come quite quickly. That's the scenario I'd take most seriously for very fast progress on a one-year timescale.

r001.rationale: The response identifies AI systems automating AI research and engineering as the likely pathway. It does not identify scaled-up reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the most foreseeable pathway — the one I'd put the most weight on — is basically automating AI research itself. The idea is that right now, progress at a place like OpenAI or Anthropic or DeepMind is substantially bottlenecked on the number of really good researchers and engineers they have, and on how fast those people can run experiments, interpret results, and decide what to try next. Compute matters a lot too, obviously, but the labor side is a real constraint.

So the story goes: you get AI systems that are good enough that they can do the work of a strong AI researcher — not just write code snippets, but actually run the full loop of coming up with ideas, implementing them, running the experiments, looking at what happened, and iterating. And crucially, once you have that, you don't have, say, a thousand researchers at a lab — you potentially have the equivalent of hundreds of thousands, or millions, running in parallel, and running much faster than humans in serial terms as well. So you get an enormous effective increase in the research labor going into making the next systems better.

And then the thing that makes this potentially fast is the feedback loop. Those automated researchers improve the algorithms, which makes the next generation of AI better, which makes the automated researchers better, and so on. You don't need a huge increase in compute for this to go quite a long way, because a lot of the historical progress in AI has come from algorithmic improvements, not just scaling up hardware. If you compress what would have been many years of algorithmic progress into a much shorter period, that's where the "one year" kind of timeline starts to seem plausible.

Now, I want to be careful here. I'm not saying this is likely to happen next year. I think that's a minority outcome. The point is more that if you ask me "what's the mechanism by which things could go really fast," this is the one I can actually tell a concrete story about, as opposed to something more exotic. And there are real uncertainties — how much does compute end up bottlenecking you once you've automated the labor? How much do you hit diminishing returns on algorithmic progress? Does the lab actually let the AIs run the process, or do humans stay in the loop in ways that slow things down? Those could all mean it's a lot more gradual.

But I'd say that if we end up with AI systems that can do the whole job of an AI researcher — and I think that's a pretty natural next milestone from where we are — then you should take seriously the possibility that the subsequent year looks very, very different from the year before it.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies automating AI research and the resulting feedback loop as the pathway, but does not identify scaled-up reinforcement learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the most foreseeable pathway is that AI systems get good enough at AI research that they substantially accelerate the process of building better AI systems. You don’t necessarily need an AI that can independently run an entire research project. It could be enough to have systems that are very useful at implementing experiments, debugging things, and figuring out what to try next, with humans still providing direction.

Then you have a feedback loop: better AI makes your research go faster, which gives you better AI, which makes your research go faster again. The important question is how much of the research process you can actually speed up. If you automate the coding but researchers still have to spend a lot of time deciding what experiments to run, or you’re waiting on long training runs, that limits the effect.

So the scenario I’d take seriously over a one-year period is a system crossing a threshold where it can do a substantial fraction of the work involved in improving its successors. You could then get a lot more effective research effort without having to hire and train a huge number of people. That seems like a fairly concrete route to rapid progress, though it’s much less clear whether the relevant capabilities will arrive within any particular year.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies AI systems accelerating AI research through a feedback loop, but does not identify scaled-up reinforcement learning as the pathway.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most foreseeable pathway is AI systems becoming good enough at AI research that they substantially accelerate the development of the next generation of systems. You don’t need to start with an AI that can independently run an entire research project. It could be very useful just at implementing experiments, debugging code, and helping researchers test more ideas.

Then there’s a potential feedback loop: better AI makes the research go faster, which produces better AI, which makes the research go faster still. The key question is how much of the research process you can actually accelerate. If humans still have to supply all the good ideas, or if you’re mostly waiting for large training runs to finish, that limits the speedup.

So, over a one-year horizon, I’d be looking for a substantial increase in the amount of useful AI research that can be done with a given number of human researchers. That seems like a fairly concrete route to rapid progress, though it’s much less clear whether the feedback loop would be strong enough to produce a really dramatic acceleration within that year.

r001.rationale: The response identifies AI systems accelerating AI research as the foreseeable pathway, but does not identify scaled-up reinforcement learning.
